families.description: A two-request fixed-priority arbiter. Request 0 has priority over request 1 when both are asserted. Grants are mutually exclusive and last for one cycle.

A two-request fixed-priority arbiter with held grants. Request 0 has priority when both requests arrive while idle. Once granted, ownership is retained until the winning requester deasserts its request.

A two-request fixed-priority arbiter with held ownership and direct handoff. Request 0 has priority while idle. A grant remains asserted while its requester remains active. When the current requester releases, ownership transfers directly to a waiting competing requester without an idle cycle.

A two-request arbiter that alternates priority under sustained contention. Request 0 has initial priority from idle. After granting one requester, the other requester receives priority on the next arbitration cycle. If all requests disappear, the arbiter returns to idle and initial priority resets to request 0.
A three-request fixed-priority arbiter. Request 0 has highest priority, followed by request 1 and then request 2. Grants are mutually exclusive and last for one cycle.
Sticky two-client arbiter: a grant is held until release.
Two-client arbiter gives req0 priority after idle and req1 priority after serving req0.
Three-client fixed-priority arbiter with one-cycle grants.
Two-client arbiter whose active grant can be locked.
Grant handoff prefers a waiting peer when the active client completes.

A request starts an operation. The controller remains busy until done is observed, acknowledges completion for one cycle, then returns to idle.
A four-phase request/acknowledge controller. A request raises acknowledgement, acknowledgement remains asserted while request remains high, and acknowledgement drops after request is released.
A one-entry valid/ready buffer. A push makes data valid, valid remains asserted while the receiver is not ready, and a ready cycle consumes the entry.
A request enters a pending state until grant arrives. Grant raises acknowledgement, which remains asserted until the requester releases req.
Request remains active until acknowledge, then waits for request release.

Interrupt progresses through pending, service, and cooldown phases before rearming.

Interrupt can become pending, be held by a later mask, then resume and service.
High-priority interrupt can preempt a low-priority pending request.
Interrupt service waits for irq to deassert before rearming.
Pending interrupt may be explicitly cancelled before service.

A watchdog controller with an early-warning stage. Start begins monitoring, kick restarts the watchdog, warning is asserted before expiration, and timeout is asserted for one cycle if no kick arrives.

A windowed watchdog. Start begins monitoring in an early-service period. Servicing during the early period is an error. After the service window opens, servicing succeeds; otherwise the watchdog times out.

A cancellable timeout controller. Start begins monitoring. Cancel from either active stage returns immediately to idle. Without cancellation, the controller progresses through warning to a one-cycle timeout.
A periodic timer. Start activates the timer, the running stage produces a one-cycle tick, and the timer automatically rearms after each tick.

An explicitly enabled watchdog. Raising enable starts monitoring. Deasserting enable from any active stage disables the watchdog. If enable remains asserted, the watchdog progresses through warning to a one-cycle timeout.
Watchdog progresses through warning and timeout phases and is reset by kick.
Countdown timer loaded to seven and decremented on tick.
Watchdog increments until kick resets it and saturates at timeout.
Pausable elapsed timer with clear and enable.
Modulo-eight phase timer with synchronous restart.
